title: Budgeting for AI coding tools
summary: Build an AI coding budget from seats, usage and API costs. Use Weave's cross-tool spending, code-level output and quality to decide what to renew.
body_markdown:
A useful AI coding budget connects what you pay with what your team ships. For subscription renewals, Weave brings cross-tool spending, adoption, code-level output and quality into the same review, so you can decide which tools to renew, expand or resize.


Start with the full bill, then review each team and tool against the work it supports.[Weave Token Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/token-intelligence) tracks supported AI-tool costs and usage.[Engineering Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/engineering-intelligence) adds consistent output measurement, review health and peer benchmarks. Together, they make the renewal conversation specific: who uses this tool, what work gets delivered, and what should next month’s budget fund?


## Build the budget from the charges you actually incur


Use this monthly starting point:


AI coding budget = seats + usage charges + direct API spend + add-ons − credits


Seats cover subscriptions. Usage charges include metered consumption and overages. Direct API spend covers separately billed provider traffic. Add-ons can include an automated reviewer or agent service. Apply discounts and credits to the charges they offset, and count each charge once. An included usage allowance belongs inside its subscription; it should not become a second expense.


Split the result by tool, team and billing owner. Keep shared organization charges visible beside the amounts assigned to people. This gives finance a complete budget and gives engineering a useful operating view.


For example, a hypothetical monthly plan could contain $2,000 in seats, $1,500 in metered usage, $500 in separate API charges and $300 in add-ons, offset by $200 in credits. The total is $4,100. These are example inputs, not vendor prices or a Weave benchmark. Replace them with your contracts and invoices.


## Review renewals by team and tool


For each renewal, collect one row with the information below. Use the same reporting period across the row.


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Field Decision it supports


Purchased seats and active users Keep, reassign or resize the subscription.


Subscription, usage and API costs Forecast the full bill and explain overages.


Code-level output and work type See what the team delivered across features, fixes and maintenance.


Review cycles, reverts and code turnover Check whether output is holding up after review and merge.


Foreground and background usage Separate interactive assistance from autonomous execution.


Cost and attribution source Understand which amounts and contributions were directly observed or estimated.


Weave supports this review across engineers, teams and tools. Per-user cost coverage includes tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Devin and Windsurf. Integration detail matters: Modal provides organization-level spend, while some tools require configured subscription costs. The[integration coverage pages](https://weaveos.com/integrations) show what each connection supplies.


Weave labels billed, reported, modeled, estimated and allocated costs. AI contribution also carries evidence from native integrations, commit metadata or activity-based estimates. Keep those labels in the review so the engineering lead and finance owner understand the basis of each result.


## Connect spending to code-aware output


The strongest renewal case shows what the investment supports. Weave analyzes pull-request changes to estimate their output in expert-hour units, considering the change’s intent, complexity, risk and dependencies. This gives the team a consistent way to compare engineering work alongside spending.


Use two complementary views: output per engineer to understand delivery, and attributed AI cost per output unit to understand spending efficiency. Weave’s[AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) explains the calculation and its inputs.


For a hypothetical team with $1,800 in attributed monthly AI spend and 450 estimated expert hours of merged output, cost per output hour is $4. Track the same calculation next month using the same team, repositories and cost sources. Keep the full organization bill alongside the attributed result.


Expert-hour units describe the work represented by a change. Use actual delivery and quality outcomes to complete the renewal decision. A team shipping more useful work with stable review health can justify a larger budget, even when its total bill increases.


## Keep interactive tools and autonomous agents visible


A coding assistant used throughout an engineer’s day serves a different workflow from an agent running tasks in the background. Weave distinguishes foreground assistance, such as interactive IDE and terminal work, from background agents executing independently.


Review each category against its job. For an interactive assistant, look at adoption, output per engineer and review friction. For a background agent, look at the work it produces, the review it requires and its associated spending. This helps you fund the workflow that earns the renewal, whether it supports an engineer directly or completes a task independently.


## Make the renewal decision concrete


Set a review date before the contract renews. Ask the team lead and budget owner to choose an action for each tool:


- **Renew:** active use supports the team’s work, spending is understood, and delivery and quality measures support keeping it.
- **Expand:** a productive workflow has broader demand. Add budget with a clear team, purpose and review date.
- **Resize or reassign:** some seats are unused or the allocation no longer matches the people doing the work.
- **Run a focused evaluation:** the team needs a clearer answer. Choose a defined workflow, a baseline and a follow-up period before making a wider commitment.


Record the decision, owner and expected change. For an evaluation, include representative code changes and feedback from the engineers using the tool. Keep staffing, repository coverage and the kind of work comparable across the review period.


## Use peer benchmarks to ask better questions


Weave’s peer benchmarks add context to output, review health and delivery. Compare an appropriate organization-size group, then inspect what explains the difference. A peer comparison can identify a useful coaching or workflow question; the team’s own trend shows whether the change helped.


The[public Weave Index](https://weaveos.com/data) and[benchmark definitions](https://weaveos.com/methodology/engineering-benchmarks) provide a starting point. Use the stated metric, period and population when bringing a benchmark into a budget discussion.


Weave’s advantage is the combined decision: cross-tool spending, code-aware output per dollar, quality and peer context. That gives an engineering leader a practical answer to “Are these coding assistant subscriptions worth renewing?” and a budget owner a clear plan for what to fund next.
